mistakes.fix: Stay in the drive and let tall happen on its own. Patience for the first five steps.
mistakes.mistake: Standing straight up out of the blocks

mistakes.fix: Push, do not reach. Quickness comes from the ground, under the hip.
mistakes.mistake: Reaching for speed with long, slow steps

mistakes.fix: Eyes stay in your lane and you sprint through the line — every rep, every race.
mistakes.mistake: Easing up before the line

mistakes.fix: Drop the shoulders and shake the hands loose behind the blocks. Loose is fast.
mistakes.mistake: Straining: clenched jaw, shoulders up in the ears

events.name: 55m / 60m
pacing: No pacing model — this race is full intent from the gun. If you are saving anything in a 55 or a 60, you have already given it away.
The 55 ends a step sooner than the 60: even less time to get tall, so the first 20 meters are the whole race.

cues: Explode on the gun — the first three steps push the track behind you.
Chin down, one straight line from head to heel.
Powerful steps, not quick little ones. Big pushes build speed.
phases.name: React & drive

cues: Let the race bring you tall — rise a little more every step.
Steps get longer and quicker at the same time.
Hands cheek to pocket. Nothing crosses the body.
phases.name: Build

cues: Tall and front-side: strike under the hip.
Loose face, loose shoulders — tension is slow.
Run through the line. The finish is five meters past it.
phases.name: Top speed, briefly

events.raceDay: Early season: attack the start at full intent and let the time be whatever it is. Championship: the same race, cleaner — no new cues, trust the start you have built.
events.tagline: The whole race is the start. There is no second half to save anything for.

mistakes.fix: Drive patience: the first steps are pushes, and tall shows up around 30m on its own.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing the drive and standing up by 15m

mistakes.fix: Strike under the hip. Reaching puts the brakes on with every step.
mistakes.mistake: Overstriding late, reaching with the lower leg

mistakes.fix: Drop the shoulders and speed the hands up. The legs follow the hands.
mistakes.mistake: Tightening up at 70m — the grimace and the shrug

mistakes.fix: Run through the line and lean at it, not before it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaning or dipping well before the line

events.name: 100m
pacing: There is no even-split 100. The second 50 is faster than the first because you are already moving — expect it, do not chase it.
By 30m you should be near 90% of your top speed. The last 40m is about protecting position and form, not finding a new gear.

cues: Push the ground back — stay low and let the rise be gradual.
Powerful steps, not frantic ones. The drive is patient aggression.
phases.name: Drive

cues: Come tall naturally. Forcing yourself upright kills the build.
Full stride now: hands cheek to pocket, strike under the hip.
phases.name: Transition

cues: This is your fastest running — tall, front-side, quick off the ground.
Relax to stay fast: loose jaw, loose shoulders, fast hands.
phases.name: Max velocity

cues: Hold your form while it burns. Do not reach for the line.
Keep the hips tall and finish through the line, not to it.
phases.name: Speed endurance

events.raceDay: Early season: run the drive honestly even if the top-end fitness is not there yet. Championship: one cue for the start, one for the finish, and nothing else in your head.
events.tagline: Build it right for 60 meters, then lose the least over the last 40.

mistakes.fix: The bend is where the race is built. Attack it — the float comes after, at speed.
mistakes.mistake: Jogging the bend to save it for the straight

mistakes.fix: First 100 at 95% feel. If the bend felt like a final, the straight will feel like a wall.
mistakes.mistake: Flying out at open-100 pace and dying at 150

mistakes.fix: Run the inside of your lane. Every step wide is extra distance you chose to run.
mistakes.mistake: Drifting wide on the bend

mistakes.fix: Stay tall and keep the knees coming through. Sitting is slowing.
mistakes.mistake: Sitting back in the last 30m

events.name: 200m
pacing: The second 100 should be faster than the first — you reach it already at full speed instead of from blocks. The split calculator below does the math for your target.
Run the first 100 hard but controlled, about 95% effort. A first 100 at open-100 pace is a loan the last 50 collects.
Indoors the 200 is a full lap: run both bends, float the back straight, and attack off the final turn. Lane draw matters more indoors — race whoever is next to you, not the clock.

cues: Drive out hard and set your lean into the bend.
First steps run the curve — body angled in, pushing along the lane.
phases.name: Drive (the bend)

cues: Come tall and carry speed around the bend.
Float means fast and relaxed — it is not rest. Let the bend run while you stay loose.
Be tall and rolling at the top of the turn. That is where the straight gets set up.
phases.name: Build & float

cues: Re-commit off the bend: quicken the arms and go again.
Hold form as it burns — knees up, hips tall, hands fast.
Finish through the line.
phases.name: Finish

events.raceDay: Early season: learn the float — most young runners get it wrong both ways, too hot or too sleepy. Championship: attack the bend, trust your fitness on the straight, and race the people next to you.
events.tagline: Attack the bend, float without slowing, finish like a sprinter.

mistakes.fix: If you are sprinting at 150, the last 100 will be a long walk home. Build first, then commit.
mistakes.mistake: Running it like a 200

mistakes.fix: Respect the race: the 300 punishes waiting. Be in the race by 150.
mistakes.mistake: Running it like a 400 — too patient early

mistakes.fix: Quicken the arms at 200 and work the bend. That is where the places move.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the race stall on the second bend

mistakes.fix: Breathe on a rhythm from the start so the last 100 is run, not survived.
mistakes.mistake: No breathing rhythm, gasping by 200

events.name: 300m
pacing: Come through 200 at about 68–70% of your total time — the split calculator below does the math for your target.
That 200 split should feel like your 400 first-200 rhythm, a touch quicker. If it feels like a 200 race, you have spent too much.
The final 100 decides it: everybody slows down. The plan is to slow down the least.

cues: Out like a 200 start — aggressive and smooth.
Settle tall by the end of the first bend.
phases.name: Drive

cues: Find your 400 rhythm early: tall, relaxed, rolling.
Breathe in rhythm. Let the race come to you a little here — without giving anything back.
phases.name: Build & settle

cues: At 200, go again: quicken the arms and work the bend.
Position matters now — do not get boxed and do not drift wide.
phases.name: Commit

cues: Speed endurance: hold your form and run through the line.
The last 50 is form, not feel.
phases.name: Finish

events.raceDay: Early season: the 300 is a fitness check — run the model and see where you stand. Championship: the break at 200 decides places, so be positioned before it, not after.
events.tagline: The in-between race: run it like a long 200 with a 400's discipline.

mistakes.fix: The first 200 has a number. Hit the number, not a feeling.
mistakes.mistake: Running a 300 and surviving a 100

mistakes.fix: The cruise is controlled speed — fast and tall. If you can chat, you are losing.
mistakes.mistake: Cruising the back straight at sightseeing pace

mistakes.fix: The bend is an attack point, not a rest. Quicken the arms at 200 and work it.
mistakes.mistake: Letting up on the second bend

mistakes.fix: Shorten up and speed the hands. Reaching is braking.
mistakes.mistake: Reaching and overstriding in the last 80

mistakes.fix: Position is won at 200–300. By the straight, you are spending what you built.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting for the home straight to start racing

events.name: 400m
pacing: The program predictor: 400 potential is about your average best 200, doubled, plus roughly 4 seconds. Work backwards from it when you set a target.
The first 200 sits about 1 to 1.5 seconds over your best 200. Much faster and the last 100 collects the debt; much slower and you have left the race out on the track.

The second 200 runs about 1.5 to 2.5 seconds slower than the first — that gap is the differential. Strength types run it closer to 1.5; speed types closer to 2.5, and the training goal is pulling that number down.
If the second 200 is more than about 3 seconds slower than the first, the first was too hot. That is a pacing error to fix, not a fitness verdict.

phases.name: Drive phase
cues: Out like a sprinter — build speed aggressively, but smooth. No panic.
You do not win the 400 in the first 50, but you can lose it there. Get out.

phases.name: Comfortable sprint
cues: Settle into a sprint that feels fast but comfortable — tall, relaxed, rolling.
Down the back straight, carry the momentum: loose hands, loose face, quick contacts.
First 200 target: your average best 200 plus about 1 to 1.5 seconds. That number is the discipline of the race.

phases.name: 2nd effort
cues: At 200, make a second effort: quicken the arms and attack the bend.
This is the deciding third: hold your position and your posture while others tie up.

phases.name: Relax
cues: Relax on purpose while the effort stays full: loose face, fast hands, technique holds.
Knees coming through, hips tall — the last 100 is run on form, not on how you feel.
Commit to the effort and run through the line.

events.raceDay: Early season: novices get a trial-and-error period in this race — run the model, tie up, learn, repeat; the splits will tell the truth. Championship: the same four efforts with full trust — chase position in the 2nd effort, not the clock.
events.tagline: A controlled sprint, run in four efforts: drive, cruise comfortably, go again, then relax and commit.

segments.note: The teaching cut — one 100 for each of the four efforts. The easiest way to hand a young runner the whole race.
Get out for 100, then two long 150s. Built for athletes who lose the middle of the race.
Isolates the drive (50), stretches the comfortable sprint (150), then splits the finish into two honest 100s.
Drive, a full 200 of the cruise, then 150 of finish. For athletes learning the back-straight discipline.

practice.title: Find the race at practice
items: Broken 400 at race pace: 200 fast, jog across the field, 200 fast.
Broken 400 at race pace: 300 fast, jog 100, 100 fast.
Broken 400 at race pace: 100 fast, jog 100, 300 fast.
250m simulations × 3–4 — the closing 250 of the race, rehearsed fresh.
The named pieces, rehearsed on their own: 100m Push (the get-out), 100m Pace (the cruise rhythm), 50m Power (the finish under fatigue).

mistakes.fix: If the baton catches you standing still, the exchange is already lost. Trust the mark and go.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving late on an exchange

mistakes.fix: Eyes forward, hand back. Looking back slows you down and moves the target.
mistakes.mistake: Looking back for the baton

mistakes.fix: One hand, one motion, practiced a hundred times. Secure first, fast second.
mistakes.mistake: Changing hands or juggling the baton in the zone

mistakes.fix: Marks only work at race speed. Every exchange rep that matters is a fast one.
mistakes.mistake: Practicing exchanges at jog speed

events.name: Relays
pacing: Order is strategy: protect a young runner on a middle leg, put racers where position gets decided, and never experiment with the order on championship day.
Relay legs run faster than open times — a running start is worth about a second on the 4×400 legs after the first. Judge legs against relay expectations, not open PRs.
Check marks are measured in practice and written down. Nobody guesses a mark on meet day.

cues: Legs: your best starter runs first, dependable hands run the middle, your best finisher anchors.
Outgoing runner: leave on the check mark and be at near-full speed when the baton arrives. Hand back steady — never look back.
Incoming runner: run through the whole zone at full speed. The baton moves to the hand; you do not slow down for it.
phases.name: Blind speed

cues: Every leg is a 200: attack the bend, float, finish. Run your own race model, not the crowd's.
Know before the meet whether your exchanges are blind or visual — and practice that one, at full speed.
Incoming runner: come in hot and loud. Outgoing runner: leave on time and show a steady hand.
phases.name: Run your 200 model

cues: The exchange is visual: the receiver watches the baton in, then goes. No blind faith.
A strong second leg matters — that is where the break and the fight for position happen.
Anchor is a race, not a victory lap: run the full 400 model, splits and all.
phases.name: Open exchange, raced legs

events.raceDay: Exchanges are decided in practice, all season. Meet day is the same marks, the same order, the same cues — a championship is the worst day to invent anything.
events.tagline: Races you win in the exchange zone. The running is the easy part.

points: Set the plan before the meet. Every athlete should leave the warm-up knowing their phases and the one job they own in each phase.
One or two cues max on race day. A race is not the time to learn five new things — pick the cue that fixes the biggest leak and let the rest ride.
After the race, grade the execution before the time. Check the splits against the plan first: a well-run race that comes up short is a fitness problem; a badly-run one is a planning problem.
The pacing numbers are models, not laws. Speed types and strength types run the same event differently — adjust the plan to the athlete in front of you.
